pedagogy.summary: Converting between units means re-expressing one measurement in a different unit of the same attribute (3 km = 3000 m, 2 hours = 120 minutes, 5 weeks = 35 days). The whole procedure hangs on one principle: the smaller the unit, the more of them you need — an inverse relationship between unit size and count — so going from a larger unit to a smaller one multiplies (the number gets bigger). It reinforces place value for the metric system (kilo = 1000) but must NOT be over-applied to time, which runs in 60s and 7s, not powers of ten.
bestPractices: Ground every conversion in the inverse relationship: a km is big, a metre is small, so one km holds MANY metres — hence larger→smaller multiplies and the count rises
Establish the relationships as secure known facts first (1000 m/km, 60 min/hr, 7 days/week), separating metric (base-ten, place value) from time (60s and 7s)
Use a two-column equivalence table so pupils see many equivalents and the pattern (repeated reasoning)
For compound/mixed measures (2 m 30 cm), convert to a common unit BEFORE combining — never string the digits together
Practise both directions and treat multiply/divide as inverse operations
keyRepresentations: The same physical length shown against two scales of different unit size (so the differing counts are visible)
A place-value chart / prefix table (kilo–, centi–, milli–) tying metric conversion to ×10 structure
A '×1000 / ÷1000 machine' making the direction of the operation explicit
A number line or tape diagram for conversion word problems
commonMisconceptions: Converts in the wrong direction — divides when the larger→smaller move should multiply, or expects the smaller-unit answer to be a smaller number
Treats a compound measure like 2 m 30 cm as one number (230, or 2.30) instead of converting and adding
Over-applies base-ten to time — an hour becomes 100 minutes
Doesn't securely know the relationship (uses 100 cm in a km, 30 days in a week)

learn.summary: Pupils (age 8-9) convert between units of the same attribute: 3 km = 3000 m, 2 hours = 120 minutes, 5 weeks = 35 days. The organising principle is the inverse relationship between unit size and count — the smaller the unit, the more of them you need — so moving from a larger unit to a smaller one multiplies and the number gets bigger. Metric conversion builds on base-ten place value (kilo = 1000), but time runs in 60s and 7s and must not be forced into powers of ten. Compound measures (2 m 30 cm) must be converted to a common unit before combining.

activities.title: One length, two scales: seeing why larger→smaller multiplies
feedback: If the learner expects the smaller-unit count to be smaller: point to the two counters — the centimetre count is always ahead of the metre count for the SAME length, because many small units fit inside one large unit.

If the learner picks the wrong gate (÷ for km→m): ask whether 3 km could really be a tiny fraction of a metre; a km is much bigger than a metre, so converting it to metres must give MANY metres (3000 m), not fewer.
If the learner uses the wrong factor (e.g. ×100 for km→m): check which pair it is — cm↔m uses 100, but m↔km uses 1000, because 1 km = 1000 m.
If correct: challenge them to predict the direction AND the factor for an unfamiliar pair before converting, naming which unit is larger.
activities.rationale: The target insight is relational (the inverse size/count relationship) and is made concrete by seeing the same length counted against two different-sized scales with the operation shown as a direction choice. An explicit live recount as the length stretches can make the inverse relationship visible, and a stated wrong-gate check anchors direction; keeping the multiplier tied to the specific pair avoids conflating cm↔m with km↔m.
sourceClaims: The Year 4 Measurement 'Big Idea' for converting units states: 'The smaller the unit, the greater the number of units needed to measure (an inverse relationship between size of unit and measure)' — the principle underlying correct conversion direction.

Year 4 pupils are taught to 'convert between different units of measure [for example, kilometre to metre; hour to minute]' and to 'solve problems involving converting from hours to minutes, minutes to seconds, years to months, weeks to days'; non-statutory guidance says they 'use multiplication to convert from larger to smaller units' and build on place value and decimal notation.

Conversion reinforces place value: 'kilo' means a thousand so 3000 m = 3 km; a kilometre is a 'unit of units' (1000 metres); and the documented root difficulty is the inverse size/count relationship (2.MD.2) — children count units and assign cardinality, arguing a row of 6 matches is 'longer' than a row of fewer larger matches.
learnerActions: Look at one physical length laid against two scales stacked together — e.g. a metre scale and a centimetre scale — each with its own counter showing how many of that unit fit the length
Make the length longer and watch BOTH counts rise, then say which count rises faster and which is always the bigger number

Explain in your own words why the smaller unit always gives the bigger count (one large unit holds many small units, so the multiplier equals how many small units fit one large unit — e.g. 100 cm in a metre)

Feed a value through a '×/÷' gate to convert between a larger and a smaller unit and back; use the km↔m case where the factor is ×1000/÷1000 because 1 km = 1000 m, and note that a different pair has a different factor (100 for cm per m)
Deliberately pick the wrong gate once and describe why the answer is an absurd size (e.g. 3 km wrongly divided to 0.003 m)
State the rule you observed: larger unit → fewer, larger units; smaller unit → more units, so larger→smaller multiplies
activities.intendedInsight: Why larger→smaller multiplies: because a larger unit holds many of the smaller unit, the smaller-unit count is always the bigger number — the inverse relationship between unit size and count, observed rather than memorised. The exact multiplier depends on the pair (100 for cm↔m, 1000 for m↔km).

activities.title: Known-facts reference: metric vs time
feedback: If the learner answers 2 hours = 200 minutes: an hour is 60 minutes, not 100 — time does not use powers of ten, so multiply by 60 (2 × 60 = 120).
If the learner uses 100 m in a km or 30 days in a week: check the reference — 1000 m in a km, 7 days in a week.
If the learner says 90 cm > 1 m because 90 > 1: the units differ; 1 m = 100 cm, so 90 cm is less than 1 m.
activities.rationale: Direction reasoning only works if the specific relationship is known, so establishing the facts first — and separating base-ten metric from time's 60s and 7s — prevents the common error of over-applying place value to time. A tap-to-reveal prefix chart can teach the facts and base-ten structure, though it cannot itself demonstrate the multiply/divide direction dynamic.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils are taught to 'convert between different units of measure [for example, kilometre to metre; hour to minute]' and to 'solve problems involving converting from hours to minutes, minutes to seconds, years to months, weeks to days'; non-statutory guidance says they 'use multiplication to convert from larger to smaller units' and build on place value and decimal notation.

Conversion reinforces place value: 'kilo' means a thousand so 3000 m = 3 km; a kilometre is a 'unit of units' (1000 metres); and the documented root difficulty is the inverse size/count relationship (2.MD.2) — children count units and assign cardinality, arguing a row of 6 matches is 'longer' than a row of fewer larger matches.
Year 5 pupils convert between different units of metric measure and use place value, multiplication and division to convert between standard units, extending to decimal notation.
learnerActions: Build and keep a reference of the relationships as secure known facts: 1000 m = 1 km, 60 seconds = 1 minute, 60 minutes = 1 hour, 7 days = 1 week
Sort the facts into two groups — metric (base-ten, follows place value: kilo = 1000) and time (60s and 7s, NOT powers of ten)
Reveal the meaning of metric prefixes (e.g. kilo = 1000, centi = one hundredth) and tie each to a worked equivalent
Answer 'which is bigger, 90 cm or 1 m?' and explain how you know, so a bigger number does not fool you
Test yourself: 'How many minutes in 2 hours?' — then explain why the answer is 120, not 100
activities.intendedInsight: Correct conversion depends on knowing the right relationship securely, and on recognising that time is not base-ten; metric and time must be kept separate.

activities.title: Compound measures: convert before combining
feedback: If the learner writes 230 straight away as if stringing digits: it works here only because 2 m = 200 cm; have them show the conversion step so they don't generalise the shortcut wrongly.

If the learner writes 2.30 cm or another mixed-up number: this treats the two units as one number; convert 2 m to 200 cm first, then add 30 cm = 230 cm (writing 2.30 m is also correct, but only with the metre unit).
If the learner adds 2 + 30 = 32 across units: 2 m and 30 cm are different units; turn the metres into centimetres before adding.
activities.rationale: Mastery tasks that refuse to total until both parts share a unit surface the compound-measure-as-single-number error, forcing the conversion step to become explicit. A builder showing the parts as blocks that won't add up until both are the same unit can make this concrete.
sourceClaims: Year 5 mastery tasks deliberately require converting mixed/compound measures to a common unit rather than combining bare numbers, e.g. the true/false task '32 cm + 1.05 m = 150 cm − 0.13 m' and combining ribbons of '1.2 m' and '90 cm' — tasks that surface the compound-measure-as-single-number error.
Year 5 pupils convert between different units of metric measure and use place value, multiplication and division to convert between standard units, extending to decimal notation.
learnerActions: Write 2 m 30 cm all in centimetres: convert the metres first (2 m = 200 cm), then add the 30 cm to get 230 cm — explaining each step
Notice that adding the numbers across units (2 + 30 = 32) or writing 2.30 cm does NOT give the length; say why (2.30 m is a correct way to write it, but only with the metre unit)
Work a mixed set and check equivalences, e.g. decide true/false for '32 cm + 1.05 m = 150 cm − 0.13 m' by converting everything to one unit first
Combine two lengths given in different units, e.g. a '1.2 m' ribbon and a '90 cm' ribbon, by converting to a common unit before adding
activities.intendedInsight: A compound measure like 2 m 30 cm is not a single number; its parts must be converted to a common unit before they can be combined.

activities.title: Both-directions conversion practice targeting common errors
feedback: If the learner divides for km→m (gives 0.003 m): a km is the larger unit, so it holds many metres — multiply (3 × 1000 = 3000 m).
If the learner multiplies for m→km: going to a larger unit means fewer, larger units — divide.
If the learner hesitates on the factor: check the known-facts reference and confirm whether the pair is metric (place value) or time (60s/7s).
activities.rationale: Conversion is a fluency procedure, and the signature errors (wrong direction, smaller-answer expectation, base-ten-for-time) make natural wrong-answer traps for learners to notice and correct during practice and self-checking. Practising both directions treats multiply/divide as inverses. Recognition-style items (spotting a wrong answer) check judgement but do not by themselves elicit independent construction, so pair them with items where the learner performs and explains the conversion.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils convert between different units of metric measure and use place value, multiplication and division to convert between standard units, extending to decimal notation.

Year 4 pupils are taught to 'convert between different units of measure [for example, kilometre to metre; hour to minute]' and to 'solve problems involving converting from hours to minutes, minutes to seconds, years to months, weeks to days'; non-statutory guidance says they 'use multiplication to convert from larger to smaller units' and build on place value and decimal notation.
learnerActions: Complete fill-in conversions in both directions: '3 km = ___ m' and '3000 m = ___ km'
Spot the wrong-direction answer, e.g. decide whether '3 km = 300 m' is right and correct it
Match equivalent measures across units and sort cards into groups of equal value
Convert 5 weeks to days and 2 hours to minutes, naming the factor used each time
Place a converted amount on a number line or tape diagram for a word problem
Explain, for one item, how you would reverse the conversion and why the operation changes (multiply ↔ divide as inverse operations)
activities.intendedInsight: Conversion is a two-way fluency procedure: multiply and divide are inverse operations, and direction is chosen by which unit is larger.

constraints: Establish the conversion relationships (1000 m/km, 60 s/min, 60 min/hr, 7 days/week) as secure known facts before drilling the procedure; a facts reference can stay to hand while the conversion direction is the focus.
Keep metric (base-ten, place value) separate from time (60s and 7s); do not over-apply powers of ten to time (an hour is 60 minutes, not 100).
The conversion multiplier is pair-specific (100 for cm↔m, 1000 for m↔km); do not let one example's factor be carried onto a different unit pair.

For compound/mixed measures, convert to a common unit BEFORE combining; never allow digits from different units to be strung together (2 m 30 cm ≠ 230 by juxtaposition — it equals 230 cm only after converting 2 m to 200 cm).

A static prefix/place-value chart with tap-to-reveal can teach the facts and base-ten structure, but pre-set content cannot itself run the live multiply/divide direction demonstration; use it as a facts scaffold, not as the main vehicle for the direction insight.
Recognition-only items (e.g. spotting a wrong conversion) assess judgement; include items where the learner constructs and explains a conversion to elicit independent production.

The manipulable two-scale demonstration is one effective way to make the inverse relationship visible; it is a proposal, not the only route — physical rulers, equivalence tables, and number lines can also make differing counts and conversion steps concrete.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and cited claims support teaching principles rather than proving any activity was tested.

The source's non-preferred artefact entries were preserved as alternatives: the prefix/place-value chart (kept as the known-facts scaffold, with its stated limit that it cannot run the direction dynamic) and the practice item types (folded into both-directions practice). The entries judged poor fit (3D interactive, in-role conversation) were dropped as not the vehicle for a numeric/relational procedure; this reflects a fit judgement and should not be read as a universal law that such media 'teach nothing'.

The original demonstration conflated cm/m scales with a km↔m ×1000 gate; this has been corrected by making the multiplier pair-specific (100 for cm↔m, 1000 for m↔km) in the activity, insight and feedback.

Self-audit of arithmetic and examples: 3 × 1000 = 3000 m ✓; 2 × 60 = 120 min ✓; 5 × 7 = 35 days ✓; 2 m = 200 cm, + 30 cm = 230 cm ✓; 1 m = 100 cm so 90 cm < 1 m ✓; wrong-gate 3 ÷ 1000 = 0.003 m shown only as an absurd error to correct. The source's own flagged errors (division giving 0.003 m, 200 min, 100 cm per km, 30 days per week) are retained only as error patterns to correct, not as valid answers.

The source's true/false equivalence task '32 cm + 1.05 m = 150 cm − 0.13 m' was kept verbatim as a mastery-style task; its truth value was not independently re-solved here — left to the teacher to verify when used (both sides appear to convert to 137 cm, so it reads TRUE, but confirm before relying on it).

Narrow affordance, not a universal law: for this numeric/relational conversion procedure an in-role dialogue partner is not itself the vehicle for performing and checking the calculations, and an added third dimension is not needed to make the inverse size/count relationship visible. These are fit judgements for media choice, not claims that such media teach nothing.

probeDeeper: 'You multiplied to turn km into m. How would you turn 3000 m back into km — and why does the operation flip?'
'Sam says 90 cm must be longer than 1 m because 90 is bigger than 1. What would you tell Sam?' (counterexample targeting the larger-number confusion)
'Why do we multiply when we go from a larger unit to a smaller one — but an hour is 60 minutes, not 100?'
'Show me how you'd write 2 m 30 cm all in centimetres, explaining each step.'
assess.correctAnswer: (1) 3 × 1000 = 3000 m — multiplies because a kilometre is the larger unit, so it holds many metres. (2) 2 × 60 = 120 min. (3) 5 × 7 = 35 days. (4) Converts the metres first — 2 m = 200 cm — then adds 30 cm to get 230 cm (not '2.30' or a strung-together '232'). Throughout, larger→smaller means multiply and the count gets bigger.

errorPatterns.pattern: Converts in the wrong direction — divides when going larger→smaller, or expects the smaller-unit answer to be a smaller number ('3 km, so a bit less than 3 metres')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor on the inverse relationship — a km is big, a metre small, so one km holds MANY metres; larger→smaller multiplies and the number grows. Show the same length against a metre scale and a km scale so the differing counts are visible.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Computes 3 ÷ 1000 for km→m, gives 0.003 m, or multiplies when going smaller→larger

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats a compound / mixed measure as a single bare number — writes 2 m 30 cm as 230 or 2.30, or adds the raw numbers across different units
errorPatterns.nextMove: Convert the metres to centimetres FIRST (2 m = 200 cm), THEN combine; use a task that won't total until both parts share a unit, as in the NCETM mixed-unit true/false tasks. Don't allow the digits to be juxtaposed.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On item (4) strings the digits together, or elsewhere adds '2 m + 30 cm = 32' without converting to a common unit

errorPatterns.pattern: Mis-recalls or mis-applies the conversion fact — including over-applying base-ten to time (an hour = 100 minutes), or 100 cm in a km, 30 days in a week
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach the specific relationships as secure known facts (60 s/min, 60 min/hr, 7 days/week, 1000 m/km) — time is NOT base-ten; keep a facts reference to hand while the conversion procedure is the focus. Scaffold rather than reteach the concept once the direction is secure.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives 2 hr = 200 min, hesitates over the factor, or uses a power of ten for a non-metric relationship

responseLevels.gap: Converts in the wrong direction or cannot decide whether to multiply or divide; strings a compound measure into a single number.
responseLevels.full: Converts reliably in both directions across metric and time units, justifying the direction by the inverse relationship (larger unit → fewer, larger units), handles compound measures by converting to a common unit first, and transfers to an unfamiliar pair.
responseLevels.partial: Converts single-unit measures when the factor is familiar (km↔m, hr↔min) but applies it mechanically — gets the direction wrong for less familiar units, over-applies base-ten to time, or cannot handle a mixed measure like 2 m 30 cm.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set a short mixed set of conversions and watch HOW the child works, not just the final numbers. (1) 'Convert 3 km into metres.' (2) 'How many minutes are there in 2 hours?' (3) 'Convert 5 weeks into days.' (4) 'A ribbon is 2 m 30 cm long. Write its length in centimetres.' Watch the direction of their operation, whether they use the right relationship, and how they treat the mixed units in (4).
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the DIRECTION catches the child who divides 3 ÷ 1000 or expects a smaller answer; item (4) catches the child who writes a compound measure as a single number rather than converting first; putting time (×60, ×7) beside metric (×1000) catches the child who over-applies base-ten and makes an hour 100 minutes.
